title: SYSK Selects: Have all the good ideas already been discovered?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun (originally 2010) asking whether all the good ideas have already been discovered. Josh introduces the episode and notes its tie-in to the planned obsolescence episode. The hosts open with banter, then cover a study on the Lower Paleolithic handle innovation and the supra marginal gyrus. They discuss claims that tech innovation has stalled (Lagarde and Verdoux on smartphones and repackaging, consolidation and refresh cycles), Edmund Phelps' views on government funding and a national innovation bank, and the NIH New Innovator Awards to Dino Di Carlo, Hu Wang (graphene cancer detection), and Jin Young Lee (optogenetic fMRI). They then move to the limits of discovery: Russell Stannard's The End of Discovery, Kant's noumenon, subjectivism and solipsism, quantum mechanics, Hawking and Mlodinow's The Grand Design, and Ramachandran's five revolutions. The episode closes with a listener email from Peyton about autocorrect and a sign-off asking for movie suggestions.

segments.title: Selects intro and show opening
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects episode from 2010 on whether all good ideas have been discovered, and the hosts open the show with banter about episode count and shrimp.

segments.title: Lower Paleolithic tools and the brain's innovation region
segments.summary: Study linking the attachment of handles to sharp stone tools, which took about two million years, to a region of the right hemisphere, the supramarginal gyrus.

segments.title: Has innovation plateaued? Charles Buell and early summation
segments.summary: The hosts frame the question of whether innovation has hit a limit, attribute a claim that everything has been invented to Charles Buell, and state that they think innovation keeps coming.

segments.title: Technological stagnation and repackaging
segments.summary: Discussion of claims by Cedric Lagarde and Eric Verdoux that tech innovation has stalled and smartphones repackage existing technology; they cover consolidation, the green boom, and short refresh cycles from Blu-ray to Super Blu-ray.

segments.title: Funding innovation: Edmund Phelps and motivation
segments.summary: Edmund Phelps argues government and big business do not fund small innovators; the hosts dispute the idea that inventors are driven by money, citing Zuckerberg and the snuggie, and Phelps's proposed national bank of innovation.

segments.title: NIH New Innovator Award
segments.summary: The hosts describe the NIH Director's New Innovator Award for early-stage ideas that lack data for a standard grant.

segments.title: 2010 New Innovator winners: Di Carlo, Wang, Lee
segments.summary: Dino Di Carlo uses magnetic nanoparticles to apply heat, pressure or chemicals to specific cell sites; Hu Wang uses one-atom-thick graphene as a biological sensor to detect cancer early; Jin Young Lee is developing optogenetic fMRI to map neuron activation beyond blood oxygen signals.

segments.title: Debate: discovery versus invention
segments.summary: The hosts debate whether the new ideas are real discoveries or variations on existing themes, and distinguish discovery from invention.

segments.title: Limits of discovery: Stannard, subjectivism, quantum mechanics
segments.summary: Russell Stannard's The End of Discovery argues human brains may reach limits; the hosts discuss Kant's noumenon, subjectivism, solipsism, and quantum observation.

segments.title: Theory of everything and the five revolutions
segments.summary: Hawking and Mlodinow's The Grand Design suggests a family of interconnected theories rather than one theory of everything; Ramachandran's five revolutions are reviewed, ending with neuroscience.

segments.title: Listener mail: Peyton and autocorrect
segments.summary: Listener Peyton jokes about autocorrect mangling texts and proposes a website of autocorrect errors; the hosts close with a request for movie suggestions.
